one_liner: Research C++ kernel for 8x8-bit product-quantization nearest-neighbour scans: keeps lookup tables in SSE registers, 4-6x faster than scalar PQ Scan.
what_it_does: Exhaustively scans one partition of 8-byte PQ codes (8 sub-quantizers of 256 centroids) for the k nearest neighbours of a query, given that query's 8x256 float distance tables. It is not a library: the repo builds two benchmark executables, pqscan (scalar, SSE, AVX and AVX2-gather variants of the classic scan on synthetic data) and pqfastscan (PQ Fast Scan versus PQ Scan on SIFT partitions). Reuse means lifting layout_partition() and scan_partition_1() from pqfastscan/, which take a pre-laid-out code buffer, a label array, the float tables and a binary heap.
how_it_is_fast: The partition is re-laid out once: codes are grouped by the high 4 bits of components 4-7 (stored once in a group header), which shrinks each code from 8 to 6 bytes, and transposed into blocks of 16 codes. Per query it builds 16-entry int8 tables (minimums over centroid groups for components 0-3, exact 4-bit sub-tables per group for components 4-7), quantized against a bound obtained by scalar-scanning the first 0.5% of codes (keep). Each block of 16 codes then gets 8 pshufb lookups and saturating int8 adds, a lower bound compared against the quantized heap bound with pcmpgtb/pmovmskb; only survivors (24,404 and 435,694 of 25.2M codes for the two README queries) are rescored with the exact float tables.
when_to_use: Exhaustive or large-partition (millions of codes) k-NN scans over 8x8-bit PQ codes with squared-L2 distance tables, on x86-64 with SSSE3.
Top-k queries with small k (the benchmark uses k = 100) where most codes can be pruned by a lower bound, so throughput comes from skipping exact rescoring.
When you need exactly the scalar ADC distances back rather than an approximation, and can afford a one-off re-layout of the database.
As a readable reference implementation of the register-resident lookup-table idea before moving to a maintained engine.
when_not_to_use: Inverted-file (IVF) indexes with many small cells: the grouping into 16^4 groups and the 0.5% scalar warm-up only pay off on large partitions; the authors' Quick ADC (4-bit codes) and Faiss IndexIVFPQFastScan target that case.
Inner-product or additive-quantization distances with negative terms: the lower-bound pruning assumes non-negative additive components (issue #2, an oracle mismatch abort on dot-product tables).
Non-x86 targets, other code sizes (only 8 sub-quantizers of 8 bits are supported, NSQ and NCENT are compile-time macros) or batched multi-query search.
Production use: research code abandoned since 2019, no library target, no tests beyond the oracle check, and it hard-links libpfm4 even for pqfastscan.

integration.dependencies: libpfm4 (linked into both benchmark executables for perf counters); CMake 2.8+ to build the benchmarks; the scan kernel itself needs only <immintrin.h> and the repo's binheap
integration.min_toolchain: C++11, g++ 4.9 recommended (the only version benchmarked; g++ 5.2 'seemed' fine, clang untested); -march=native -ffast-math -Werror in CMakeLists
integration.platforms: x86-64 Linux with SSE2, SSE3, SSSE3 and POPCNT (AVX/AVX2 only for the baseline variants in pqscan)
integration.thread_safety: not documented; scan_partition_1 increments global non-atomic Counters::total_scan and writes Counters::quant_bound, so concurrent scans race on those counters
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial: the result heap matches PQ Scan's distances, but the database must be re-laid out (grouped and interleaved) and labels come from a permutation array the caller must keep

gotchas: Label bug in the shipped code: layout_partition() groups only the codes after the first 'keep' codes but permutes the identity array starting at index 0, and fast_scan_1() reports labels[i] without adding keep, so every neighbour found outside the first 0.5% of the partition is returned with an ID too small by keep (125,797 in the README run). The benchmark's oracle check compares only distances (tolerance 0.1), so it never catches this; timing is unaffected.

Exactness depends on a strict test: candidates are kept only if the sum of floor-quantized int8 lower bounds is strictly below the floor-quantized heap bound, so a code whose true distance is just under the bound can in principle be pruned when the smallest table entry (qmin) is near zero; the 7*qmin slack from per-component offsets usually hides this, and the benchmark aborts on any mismatch (reading of fastscan.cpp, not observed in a run).

The published pqfastscan rows are single runs (repeat = 1, gettimeofday) per query with PQ Scan always timed first; speedup varies by query with the number of survivors (6.1x with 24,404 rescored codes, 4.3x with 435,694).

pqscan needs root for perf counters and requests Intel-only events (CYCLE_ACTIVITY:CYCLES_LDM_PENDING and others); on other CPUs it fails until those events are removed (issue #1). Dataset links on assets.xion345.info no longer resolve (issue #3).
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Among the catalogued SIMD libraries only its sibling Quick ADC addresses the same problem; pick PQ Fast Scan when you need exact 8x8-bit PQ distances over large partitions, and Quick ADC when you scan many small IVF cells and accept 4-bit codes with a small recall loss.
verified_claims_summary: The authors' own scalar PQ Scan (8 float-table lookups per code plus heap) versus PQ Fast Scan on 25.2M-code ANN_SIFT100M1 partitions with ANN_SIFT1B queries, k = 100, keep = 0.5%: README rows give 75,392 vs 12,272 us and 74,754 vs 17,480 us (about 6.1x and 4.3x, derived from page data), consistent with the README's 4-6x and the PVLDB 9(4) paper (snippet only, which reports 4-6x across Intel CPUs released 2009-2014); built with g++ 4.9 -O3 -march=native -ffast-math, CPU model not stated on any reachable page.
status_note: Abandoned since 2019-05-31 (26 commits, 70 stars) but Clear-BSD-licensed and small enough to lift two source files from; fix the keep label offset before using its neighbour IDs, or use Faiss's maintained 4-bit FastScan indexes instead.
